passage:
For much of the twentieth century, historians of the French Revolution worked under the long shadow of the thesis associated with Georges Lefebvre. According to Lefebvre's classic account, the Revolution is best understood as a bourgeois revolution: an ascendant commercial and professional class, frustrated by a political order that still privileged the nobility, moved decisively in 1789 to sweep away feudal constraints and install a regime congenial to its economic interests. The narrative had the virtue of coherence — it explained why the Revolution happened when it did, who its principal beneficiaries were, and why it took the legal forms it took — and for two generations textbooks echoed it with minor variations.

That consensus began to erode in the 1960s, when the historian Alfred Cobban argued that Lefebvre's bourgeoisie was a category with little empirical content. Examining the occupations of the deputies elected to the Estates-General in 1789, Cobban found that the Third Estate's representatives were, for the most part, not capitalist merchants or industrialists but office-holders, lawyers, and professionals — a group whose wealth was drawn from venal offices and landed rents rather than from trade or manufacture. If these men were the revolutionaries, Cobban contended, then the Revolution could not be explained as the political triumph of a rising commercial class; it had to be explained in other terms, perhaps as a conflict internal to the propertied elite over access to the state.

Cobban's challenge has not gone unanswered, and the picture that has emerged over the last several decades is less tidy than either his account or Lefebvre's. Subsequent social historians, working with parish registers, notarial archives, and tax rolls, have shown that the boundary between commercial and office-holding wealth in eighteenth-century France was more porous than Cobban's prosopography suggested: a successful merchant often bought offices for his sons, and an office-holding family often maintained an interest in trade. What has fallen away, however, is any confident identification of the Revolution with the interests of a single coherent class. In its place stands a more cautious formulation: that the Revolution emerged from a shifting coalition of groups whose members shared grievances against the old regime without sharing a unified economic program. This reformulation preserves what was durable in Lefebvre's attention to social structure while accepting the force of Cobban's evidence that the social structure in question was not simply bourgeois. The cost of the reformulation is a loss of narrative drive. What it offers in return is a version of the Revolution that the sources will actually support.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Georges Lefebvre's bourgeois-revolution thesis, long accepted as the definitive account of the French Revolution, has been conclusively refuted by later social historians.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alfred Cobban's demonstration that the deputies of the Third Estate were not capitalists showed that class analysis has no role to play in the history of the French Revolution.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cobban's empirical challenge to Lefebvre has led not to outright rejection of Lefebvre's attention to social structure but to a more cautious account of the Revolution as emerging from a coalition of groups without a unified economic program.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recent work in parish registers, notarial archives, and tax rolls has shown that the boundary between commercial and office-holding wealth in eighteenth-century France was more porous than earlier historians supposed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Narrative coherence, rather than empirical support, is the principal virtue that has recommended Lefebvre's interpretation of the French Revolution to generations of textbook writers.

explanations.correct: The passage sets up Lefebvre (paragraph 1), presents Cobban's challenge (paragraph 2), and settles on a synthesis (paragraph 3) that 'preserves what was durable in Lefebvre's attention to social structure while accepting the force of Cobban's evidence.' C captures both halves.
explanations.A: Overstated: the passage says Lefebvre's attention to social structure is preserved, not refuted.
explanations.B: Reverses the passage: class analysis survives in a revised form.
explanations.D: Too narrow — the archival detail is one piece of evidence for a broader reformulation.
explanations.E: Paragraph-level restatement that promotes a coda about narrative drive to the thesis.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A historical thesis is introduced; an empirical challenge to it is presented; a qualified synthesis is endorsed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two historians' views are summarized; a third view is shown to be superior to both; the limitations of the third view are catalogued.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A methodological dispute is sketched; the contending parties are named; the dispute is declared insoluble on present evidence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A long-standing consensus is defended against a recent challenge, which is shown to rest on a misreading of its principal sources.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A class analysis is applied to one historical event, then extended to two additional events, and finally generalized into a theory of revolution.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 presents Lefebvre's thesis; paragraph 2 presents Cobban's empirical challenge; paragraph 3 endorses a qualified synthesis. A matches each move in order.
explanations.B: Mis-sequences: the synthesis is not a third view superior to both; it integrates elements of each.
explanations.C: The passage treats the dispute as productive, not insoluble.
explanations.D: Reverses the author's direction: Cobban's challenge is granted force, not rebutted.
explanations.E: Only one event (the French Revolution) is considered.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, Cobban's examination of the deputies elected to the Estates-General in 1789 revealed that the representatives of the Third Estate were

choices.label: A
choices.text: chiefly capitalist merchants and industrialists whose interests lay in overseas trade

choices.label: B
choices.text: for the most part office-holders, lawyers, and professionals whose wealth came from venal offices and landed rents

choices.label: C
choices.text: drawn almost equally from the commercial bourgeoisie and the remnants of the feudal nobility

choices.label: D
choices.text: primarily tenant farmers with grievances against the seigneurial system

choices.label: E
choices.text: a mixture of urban artisans and rural clergy who shared a common hostility to the monarchy

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states that Cobban found the Third Estate's representatives 'were, for the most part, not capitalist merchants or industrialists but office-holders, lawyers, and professionals — a group whose wealth was drawn from venal offices and landed rents.'
explanations.A: Reverses what Cobban found; this is the Lefebvrian picture he challenged.
explanations.C: Plausible-world detail the passage never supplies.
explanations.D: Out of scope; the passage does not discuss tenant farmers.
explanations.E: Out of scope; urban artisans and rural clergy are not mentioned.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the reformulation described in the final paragraph is best characterized as

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement of an account that has resolved the disputes among earlier historians

choices.label: B
choices.text: cautious approval, tempered by recognition that the new account sacrifices narrative drive

choices.label: C
choices.text: skepticism about a compromise position that evades the choice between Lefebvre and Cobban

choices.label: D
choices.text: detached neutrality toward a reformulation whose acceptance remains in dispute

choices.label: E
choices.text: frustration that the reformulation has failed to satisfy readers who prefer Lefebvre's clarity

explanations.correct: The author credits the reformulation with preserving what was durable in Lefebvre and accepting what was forceful in Cobban, and closes by saying it offers 'a version of the Revolution that the sources will actually support' — clear approval. The passage also flags the 'cost' of lost narrative drive. Cautious approval, tempered by that acknowledgment, is exactly B.
explanations.A: Overstates: the passage explicitly notes a cost.
explanations.C: Opposite direction: the author treats the compromise as disciplined by evidence, not as evasion.
explanations.D: The final paragraph takes a clear evaluative position.
explanations.E: Frustration is not the tone; the author accepts the loss of drive as the price of fidelity to sources.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of parish registers, notarial archives, and tax rolls in the final paragraph functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate the kinds of sources that have enabled historians to complicate Cobban's prosopographic picture of eighteenth-century French wealth

choices.label: B
choices.text: argue that Cobban's reliance on occupational data alone has been decisively repudiated by specialists in archival research

choices.label: C
choices.text: introduce a methodological digression on the documentary resources available for the study of eighteenth-century France

choices.label: D
choices.text: provide evidence that the French Revolution was indeed the political triumph of a rising commercial class, contrary to Cobban

choices.label: E
choices.text: demonstrate that later social historians have relied on a wider range of sources than Lefebvre or Cobban did

explanations.correct: The archival sources appear in the sentence that says the boundary between commercial and office-holding wealth 'was more porous than Cobban's prosopography suggested.' Their function is to illustrate the evidence that has blurred that boundary.
explanations.B: Too strong: the passage says the picture has been complicated, not that Cobban has been 'decisively repudiated' — and the final paragraph preserves the force of his evidence.
explanations.C: Wrong grain: the mention is not a digression but a compressed evidentiary citation.
explanations.D: Reverses the passage: the new evidence does not restore the Lefebvrian thesis.
explanations.E: Accurate content, wrong function: the point is not a source comparison but a correction to Cobban's specific claim.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements about Lefebvre's account of the French Revolution?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It should be dismissed as an artifact of the ideological commitments of an earlier generation of historians.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Its attention to the social composition of the revolutionary movement remains valuable, even though its identification of that composition as straightforwardly bourgeois has not held up.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Its principal weakness was a failure to consult the notarial and parish records that later historians would exploit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It correctly identified the Third Estate's deputies as representatives of a rising commercial class.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its coherence as a narrative outweighs any empirical difficulties that have been raised against it.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 says the reformulation 'preserves what was durable in Lefebvre's attention to social structure while accepting the force of Cobban's evidence that the social structure in question was not simply bourgeois.' B is a precise paraphrase of that endorsement-with-qualification.
explanations.A: Too strong: the passage preserves something of Lefebvre, not dismisses him.
explanations.C: The passage does not blame Lefebvre for not using sources that became central in later work.
explanations.D: Reverses the passage: the Third Estate deputies were not, on Cobban's evidence, a rising commercial class.
explanations.E: Inverts the author's priorities: the passage accepts loss of narrative drive as the cost of empirical fidelity.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the reformulated account of the French Revolution described in the final paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A newly discovered set of merchant ledgers shows that commercial profits in eighteenth-century France were larger than previously estimated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A systematic study of the cahiers de doléances reveals that grievances against the old regime were voiced with equal intensity by office-holders, merchants, and professionals but diverged sharply when remedies were proposed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Parish registers demonstrate that population growth in French cities outpaced that in the countryside during the decades preceding 1789.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A monograph on a single province shows that its Third Estate delegation consisted almost entirely of capitalist merchants.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Contemporary pamphleteers used the word 'bourgeois' in a sense broad enough to include office-holders and professionals.

explanations.correct: The reformulated account holds that the Revolution emerged from 'a shifting coalition of groups whose members shared grievances against the old regime without sharing a unified economic program.' Evidence that grievances were shared across occupational categories but that proposed remedies diverged is precisely the pattern that coalition-without-unified-program predicts.
explanations.A: Off-target: larger commercial profits would tend to revive a Lefebvrian reading, not support the coalition account.
explanations.C: Demographic trends do not speak to the coalition claim.
explanations.D: Would support Lefebvre, not the reformulated account.
explanations.E: Addresses vocabulary, not whether the coalition shared an economic program.

passage:
For most of the twentieth century, sociologists who studied the professions treated them as an unambiguous good. On the influential account developed by Talcott Parsons in the 1940s and refined by his students, an occupation such as medicine or law earned the title of profession by virtue of a trio of features: a body of esoteric knowledge acquired through long training, a set of ethical standards that bound practitioners to serve clients' interests rather than their own, and a system of collegial self-regulation that prevented abuse of the specialized authority clients had to grant. On this reading, professional autonomy was the price society paid, and should pay willingly, for competent and disinterested service.

That picture was challenged in the 1970s by a group of sociologists — Eliot Freidson, Magali Larson, and Andrew Abbott among the most prominent — who argued that Parsons had mistaken the professions' self-description for their sociological reality. On this revisionist view, professions are better understood as occupational groups that have successfully organized to secure control over a segment of the labor market. The esoteric knowledge is real, but it also serves as an entry barrier; the ethical code is real, but it also legitimates the group's claim to exclude outsiders; and self-regulation, whatever its protections, also insulates members from the kinds of accountability imposed on ordinary workers. Where Parsons saw a functional exchange, the revisionists saw an exercise of power, achieved through what Larson called a 'professional project' of market closure.

Recent scholarship has tried to hold both accounts in view. The revisionists were surely right that Parsons understated the interests served by professional organization, and case studies of medicine, law, and accountancy in the twentieth century repeatedly find episodes in which professional bodies acted to exclude competitors or to shield members from outside scrutiny. But a purely market-closure account has trouble explaining why clients, regulators, and the wider public continue to treat professional claims seriously, and why the most egregious failures of self-regulation — when they are exposed — generate the kind of scandal that treats betrayal, rather than mere self-interest, as the appropriate category. That reaction makes sense only if the service-oriented commitments Parsons described are still, to some degree, believed. The professions, on the current reading, are neither the selfless institutions of functionalist description nor the naked cartels of the revisionist counter-picture; they are hybrid arrangements whose legitimacy depends on a plausible performance of disinterest even when the incentives for self-dealing are strong.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Talcott Parsons's functionalist account of the professions has been conclusively refuted by the market-closure analyses of Freidson, Larson, and Abbott.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because self-regulation has so often failed in medicine, law, and accountancy, professions should be subjected to the same accountability mechanisms as ordinary occupations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The sociology of the professions has moved from a functionalist picture of disinterested service, through a revisionist picture of market closure, toward a hybrid account on which legitimacy depends on a plausible performance of disinterest.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Magali Larson's concept of the 'professional project' has become the dominant analytic framework for understanding the development of the modern professions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Scandals involving failures of professional self-regulation demonstrate that the public's faith in the professions' ethical commitments has been systematically misplaced.

explanations.correct: The passage traces three views in order — Parsons's functionalism (paragraph 1), the revisionist market-closure account (paragraph 2), and a hybrid synthesis (paragraph 3) on which professional legitimacy depends on a 'plausible performance of disinterest.' C captures all three moves.
explanations.A: Overstated: the passage says the revisionists were 'surely right' on one point, not that Parsons has been refuted.
explanations.B: Too strong and outside scope: the author does not recommend accountability reforms.
explanations.D: Too narrow: Larson's term is one element in a broader analytic development.
explanations.E: Paragraph-level restatement that misreads the author, who treats public reaction to scandals as evidence that the service-oriented commitments are still believed.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, Parsons's account identified which one of the following as among the defining features of a profession?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Credentialing examinations administered by the state rather than by the professional body itself

choices.label: B
choices.text: A body of esoteric knowledge acquired through long training

choices.label: C
choices.text: An openness to competitive entry from adjacent occupations

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fees calibrated to the market rate of comparable unskilled labor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Public oversight of individual disciplinary proceedings

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 lists the trio of features Parsons identified: 'a body of esoteric knowledge acquired through long training,' 'a set of ethical standards,' and 'a system of collegial self-regulation.'
explanations.A: Reverses Parsons's picture: self-regulation, not state credentialing, is the feature he named.
explanations.C: Contradicts Parsons: his picture emphasized controlled entry, not openness.
explanations.D: Out of scope; fees are not discussed.
explanations.E: Contradicts Parsons: self-regulation excluded external oversight of discipline.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the revisionist account developed by Freidson, Larson, and Abbott is best described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: unreserved endorsement of an account that has definitively replaced Parsons's functionalism

choices.label: B
choices.text: respect for its corrective insight, tempered by judgment that on its own it cannot explain the public's sustained reaction to professional scandals

choices.label: C
choices.text: dismissal of a polemical critique whose conclusions have not survived subsequent case-study work

choices.label: D
choices.text: neutrality toward a view whose prospects the author declines to evaluate

choices.label: E
choices.text: sharp disagreement rooted in a preference for Parsons's earlier formulation

explanations.correct: The author says the revisionists 'were surely right' that Parsons understated interests, but argues that a 'purely market-closure account has trouble explaining' the public's scandal reaction. That is respect plus a limitation — exactly B.
explanations.A: Overstates: the passage denies that the revisionist view alone suffices.
explanations.C: Opposite valence: the author credits the revisionists.
explanations.D: The final paragraph takes a clear evaluative stance.
explanations.E: The author also credits the revisionists against Parsons; no preference for Parsons is expressed.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of public reaction to 'the most egregious failures of self-regulation' (in paragraph 3) functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: concede that professional self-regulation has failed so often that the functionalist picture can no longer be defended

choices.label: B
choices.text: supply evidence that the service-oriented commitments Parsons described are, to some degree, still believed and therefore not reducible to market closure

choices.label: C
choices.text: illustrate the political difficulties that professional bodies face when their internal disputes become public

choices.label: D
choices.text: distinguish the accountancy profession, which has experienced more public scandal, from medicine and law

choices.label: E
choices.text: argue that scandal, rather than routine regulation, is the most effective mechanism for disciplining the professions

explanations.correct: The author says the scandal reaction 'makes sense only if the service-oriented commitments Parsons described are still, to some degree, believed.' The reference is offered as evidence that the revisionist market-closure account is incomplete.
explanations.A: Reverses the author's conclusion: the scandal reaction is taken to show Parsons's picture is still partly operative.
explanations.C: Wrong grain: the passage is interested in public reaction, not in professional bodies' political difficulties.
explanations.D: No distinction among medicine, law, and accountancy is drawn in the passage.
explanations.E: Outside scope; the passage does not recommend scandal as a disciplinary mechanism.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that, on the author's current reading, a profession could lose its claim to legitimacy if

choices.label: A
choices.text: its members were required, for the first time, to acquire their knowledge through long formal training

choices.label: B
choices.text: competing occupations were permitted to perform tasks previously reserved to it

choices.label: C
choices.text: the service-oriented performance on which its authority rests ceased to be plausible to clients, regulators, and the wider public

choices.label: D
choices.text: sociologists convinced the public that the revisionist account was entirely correct and Parsons's account entirely wrong

choices.label: E
choices.text: the profession's ethical code were codified in state statute rather than in the profession's own charter

explanations.correct: The final paragraph says professions are 'hybrid arrangements whose legitimacy depends on a plausible performance of disinterest.' If that performance ceased to be plausible to the relevant audiences, legitimacy would, on the author's account, fail. C is a hedged paraphrase.
explanations.A: Out of scope; the passage does not treat the introduction of formal training as a legitimacy threshold.
explanations.B: Off-target: market-closure competition is one pressure but not what the author identifies as the condition of legitimacy.
explanations.D: The passage concerns sociological analysis, not whether public opinion about sociology affects legitimacy.
explanations.E: Out of scope; statutory codification is not addressed.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations is most closely analogous to the 'hybrid arrangement' the author attributes to the professions in the final paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A charitable foundation that raises funds solely to deliver services to those in need, and that discloses all expenditures in an audited annual report.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A cartel of manufacturers that fixes prices through secret agreements, deriving its profits entirely from the elimination of competition.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A judicial body whose authority over the parties before it depends on their continued belief in its impartiality, and whose exclusive jurisdiction also shields its members from outside review.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A publicly traded corporation whose directors are elected by shareholders and whose financial performance is monitored by regulators.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A labor union whose members negotiate wages collectively and whose internal discipline is enforced by elected officers.

explanations.correct: The author's principle is that legitimacy depends on a plausible performance of disinterest even when the insider group also enjoys the advantages of market closure. A judicial body whose authority rests on perceived impartiality while its exclusive jurisdiction insulates its members is a close instance of that dual structure.
explanations.A: Matches only the service-oriented half; no closure-like insulation is described.
explanations.B: Matches only the closure half, with no service-oriented performance that could fail or succeed.
explanations.D: Corporate governance involves shareholder monitoring and external regulation — accountability mechanisms the passage explicitly contrasts with professional self-regulation.
explanations.E: A union bargains on behalf of its own members; no claim of disinterested service to clients or the public is in play.

questions.questionStem: The phrase 'professional project' as used in the passage most nearly refers to

choices.label: A
choices.text: a coordinated program of research in which members of a profession define their field's central problems

choices.label: B
choices.text: an organized effort by an occupational group to secure control over a segment of the labor market

choices.label: C
choices.text: the long course of formal training that produces a profession's esoteric knowledge

choices.label: D
choices.text: an individual practitioner's career plan for moving from apprentice to senior status

choices.label: E
choices.text: a government initiative aimed at bringing new occupations under professional regulation

explanations.correct: The term is introduced in paragraph 2 alongside 'market closure': 'an exercise of power, achieved through what Larson called a professional project of market closure.' The contextual sense is the organized effort to secure labor-market control.
explanations.A: Common-meaning trap: in ordinary usage 'project' can mean a research program, but the passage uses the term in Larson's narrower sense.
explanations.C: Conflates 'professional project' with one of the features (training) rather than the market-closure effort.
explanations.D: Wrong grain: the term names a collective phenomenon, not an individual career plan.
explanations.E: Reverses agency: in the passage, the project is the occupational group's own, not a government initiative.
